Hadadrimmon
HAY-dad-RIM-on
proper n. (place in the valley of Megiddon; a byword for great mourning)
Hebrew hadad rimmon, joining the names of two Syrian storm-gods, Hadad and Rimmon; most likely the name of a town in the plain of Megiddo.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Zechariah compares the coming repentance of Jerusalem to the greatest mourning in Israel's memory. The LORD promises to pour the spirit of grace and supplications on the house of David, so that they look on Him whom they pierced and mourn. Then: “In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon” (Zechariah 12:11). The reference is almost certainly to the death of Josiah, the last good king of Judah, struck down at Megiddo: “And all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah” (2 Chronicles 35:24). “And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day” (2 Chronicles 35:25). Zechariah takes that national grief over a fallen king and says it will be matched by Israel's grief over the pierced Shepherd, a mourning John sees fulfilled at the cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Hadadrimmon; the name is that of a place in the valley of Megiddo, carried into the Authorized Version from the original.

expand to see more

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Hadadrimmon.

The name joins Hadad and Rimmon, names of Syrian deities.

It is most likely a town in the plain of Megiddo.

It occurs once, at Zechariah 12:11.

The mourning there is commonly referred to the death of Josiah.

Key Scripture

Zec 12:11 — "In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon."

2Ch 35:24 — "His servants therefore took him out of that chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had; and they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died, and was buried in one of the sepulchres of his fathers. And all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah."

2Ch 35:25 — "And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day, and made them an ordinance in Israel: and, behold, they are written in the lamentations."

Modern Corruption

Hadadrimmon is read as a pagan rite of mourning for a dying god, when the setting points to Israel's mourning for Josiah at Megiddo.

expand to see more

Because the name joins two divine names, some commentators make the mourning of Hadadrimmon a ritual lament for a fertility deity, like the weeping for Tammuz. Jerome identified it as a town near Megiddo, and the link with Josiah's death in the valley of Megiddo fits Zechariah's comparison of a national mourning for a king.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is evangelical repentance. Zechariah's mourning flows from grace poured out, not from despair, and it looks upon the pierced One (John 19:37).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hadad rimmon, two Syrian divine names; a place near Megiddo, scene of the mourning for Josiah.

expand to see more

Hadad, a Syrian storm-god; Rimmon, a related deity.

Zechariah 12:10 promises the spirit of grace and supplications.

Zechariah 12:11 compares the mourning to that of Hadadrimmon.

2 Chronicles 35:24-25 records the mourning for Josiah.

John 19:37 cites Zechariah of the pierced Christ.

Usage

"the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon"

"the nation's grief for Josiah"

"mourning for the pierced One"
